description: Verified public-domain quotes, poems and passages for original comics in the style of Zen Pencils. Sorted by comic_potential (highest first), then by whether Zen Pencils has not adapted the author (unadapted first); ties keep curator order, with quotes already used in this project last.

quotes.text: "When I found I had crossed dat line," she said, "I looked at my hands to see if I was de same pusson. There was such a glory ober ebery ting; de sun came like gold through the trees, and ober the fields, and I felt like I was in Heaben."
quotes.popular_text: When I found I had crossed that line, I looked at my hands to see if I was the same person. There was such a glory over everything; the sun came like gold through the trees, and over the fields, and I felt like I was in Heaven.
quotes.author: Harriet Tubman (as told to Sarah H. Bradford)
quotes.work: Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman, by Sarah H. Bradford
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1869; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: A wordless, blue-grey night sequence follows a woman wading through Maryland swamps by the North Star; at an unmarked line of trees the palette floods gold and she stares at her own hands like a stranger's, then the last panel shows her turning south again, lantern shuttered, to go back for her family.
quotes.notes: Tubman could not write; Bradford recorded her words in dialect. Popular versions standardise the spelling. Many other 'Tubman quotes' online are misattributed (see README).

quotes.text: I, who began to think they would not go out, after all their talk, became impatient, and started on ahead, saying, with childish bravado, "I don't care what you do, I am going to turn out, whether any one else does or not;" and I marched out, and was followed by the others.
quotes.author: Harriet Hanson Robinson
quotes.work: Loom and Spindle; or, Life Among the Early Mill Girls (recalling the 1836 Lowell mill strike, when she was 11)
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1898; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: An 11-year-old bobbin girl in an 1836 Lowell cotton mill watches grown women whisper about a strike and then freeze at their looms; she marches alone down the long aisle past the overseer, and the page turn shows the whole floor of women filing down the stairs behind her.
quotes.notes: Working-class and child-labour voice; the 'I' was italicised in the original.

quotes.text: ¿qué podemos saber las mujeres sino filosofías de cocina? Bien dijo Lupercio Leonardo, que bien se puede filosofar y aderezar la cena. Y yo suelo decir viendo estas cosillas: Si Aristóteles hubiera guisado, mucho más hubiera escrito.
quotes.popular_text: If Aristotle had cooked, he would have written much more.
quotes.author: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
quotes.work: Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz (letter)
quotes.translator: english_gloss is our own literal translation (no public-domain English translation was found)
quotes.english_gloss: What can we women know, except kitchen philosophies? Lupercio Leonardo put it well: one can philosophise perfectly well while making supper. And seeing these little things I often say: if Aristotle had cooked, he would have written much more.
quotes.verification_level: primary transcription on a reliable site
quotes.public_domain_reason: Written 1691, first printed 1700; author died 1695. Public domain everywhere.
quotes.story_seed: A nun in a 1690s Mexico City convent, forbidden her books, is sent to the kitchen as punishment; panel by panel the eggs frying in oil, syrup threads and spinning tops turn into chalk diagrams across the kitchen walls, and the turn is the Mother Superior arriving to scold her and staying up all night with the equations.
quotes.notes: Text is in the original Spanish. Verified against the marxists.org transcription (its accented characters are damaged in the page encoding; wording matches). Use a fresh translation for the comic.

quotes.text: I finally concluded that all failure was from a wobbling will rather than a wobbling wheel.
quotes.author: Frances E. Willard
quotes.work: A Wheel Within a Wheel: How I Learned to Ride the Bicycle
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1895; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: A 53-year-old widowed seamstress learns to ride her dead son's bicycle in the tenement courtyard at dawn; her twenty falls are drawn as a tally chart scratched on the wall, the turn comes when she stops staring at the cobbles and fixes her eyes on the far gate, and the last panel has her pedalling past the factory girls on their walk to work.
quotes.notes: Willard learned to ride at 53. A women's-cycling story, close to sport.

quotes.text: To young men contemplating a voyage I would say go. The tales of rough usage are for the most part exaggerations, as also are the stories of sea danger.
quotes.author: Joshua Slocum
quotes.work: Sailing Alone Around the World
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1900; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: A 70-year-old harbour-master who has spent forty years logging other people's departures (and warning them off) writes his own name in the outbound ledger, rows a patched dinghy past the breakwater while the young sailors he lectured line the pier, and the final panel flips his old sign NO SMALL CRAFT BEYOND THIS POINT to show he has painted GO on the back.
quotes.notes: Slocum was the first person to sail alone around the world (1895-98).

quotes.text: I am an enthusiast, but not a crank in the sense that I have some pet theories as to the proper construction of a flying machine. I wish to avail myself of all that is already known and then if possible add my mite to help on the future workers who will attain final success.
quotes.author: Wilbur Wright
quotes.work: Letter to the Smithsonian Institution, 30 May 1899
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Private letter written 1899; author died 1912, so public domain (life+70), and it has long been printed and held in the Smithsonian archives.
quotes.story_seed: A shy teenage girl in a small-town bike repair shop mails a handwritten letter to a university asking for 'everything you have on flight'; a crate of dusty pamphlets arrives, and the story follows her studying at night between tyre repairs until the last page shows her kite-glider lifting off the dunes while the professor who sent the crate reads about it in the newspaper.
quotes.notes: The letter that started the Wright brothers' research.

quotes.text: Once upon a time, I, Chuang Tzŭ, dreamt I was a butterfly, fluttering hither and thither, to all intents and purposes a butterfly. I was conscious only of following my fancies as a butterfly, and was unconscious of my individuality as a man. Suddenly, I awaked, and there I lay, myself again. Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I am a man.
quotes.author: Chuang Tzu (Zhuangzi)
quotes.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, tr. Herbert A. Giles, ch. II
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Ancient text; Giles translation published 1889 (translator died 1935). Public domain.
quotes.story_seed: An overworked accountant dozes at his desk in a Hong Kong tower and spends a whole wordless double page as a butterfly over the harbour; he wakes to find wing-dust on his fingertips, and the final panel cuts to a butterfly asleep on a leaf, dreaming of spreadsheets.

zp_adapted_quote.note: Zen Pencils adapted Lao Tzu (#18, #165), not Chuang Tzu.

quotes.notes: Zen Pencils adapted Lao Tzu, but not Chuang Tzu.

quotes.text:
Does the road wind up-hill all the way?
   Yes, to the very end.
Will the day's journey take the whole long day?
   From morn to night, my friend.

But is there for the night a resting-place?
   A roof for when the slow dark hours begin.
May not the darkness hide it from my face?
   You cannot miss that inn.

Shall I meet other wayfarers at night?
   Those who have gone before.
Then must I knock, or call when just in sight?
   They will not keep you standing at that door.

Shall I find comfort, travel-sore and weak?
   Of labour you shall find the sum.
Will there be beds for me and all who seek?
   Yea, beds for all who come.
quotes.author: Christina Rossetti
quotes.work: Up-Hill (Goblin Market and Other Poems)
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1862; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: A small girl and her grandfather climb the endless switchback stairs of a Lisbon hillside at dusk, she asking each question and he answering; he carries her up the last flight, and at the top a door swings open on a lamp-lit table crowded with every relative who climbed before, her grandmother's chair pulled out for him.
quotes.notes: Complete poem, 16 lines.

quotes.text: That was all of tangible things; but in memories we were rich. We had pierced the veneer of outside things. We had "suffered, starved, and triumphed, grovelled down yet grasped at glory, grown bigger in the bigness of the whole." We had seen God in His splendours, heard the text that Nature renders. We had reached the naked soul of man.
quotes.author: Ernest Shackleton
quotes.work: South: The Story of Shackleton's Last Expedition, 1914-1917
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1919; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: A grandmother empties a battered biscuit tin onto the kitchen table for a grandson who says her life was 'boring': a cracked compass, one frozen mitten, a spoon bent into a hook; each object opens a panel of the winter she spent snowed in at a remote weather station, and the boy ends up asking to keep the tin.
quotes.notes: The words in inner quotation marks are Shackleton quoting Robert Service's 'The Call of the Wild'. The famous 'Men wanted for hazardous journey' newspaper ad is apocryphal and was dropped.

quotes.text:
Come, my friends,
'Tis not too late to seek a newer world.
Push off, and sitting well in order smite
The sounding furrows; for my purpose holds
To sail beyond the sunset, and the baths
Of all the western stars, until I die.
It may be that the gulfs will wash us down:
It may be we shall touch the Happy Isles,
And see the great Achilles, whom we knew.
Tho' much is taken, much abides; and tho'
We are not now that strength which in old days
Moved earth and heaven; that which we are, we are;
One equal temper of heroic hearts,
Made weak by time and fate, but strong in will
To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.
quotes.author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
quotes.work: Ulysses (Poems, 1842), lines 56-70
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1842; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: Four retired lifeboat crew in their eighties break their decommissioned rowing lifeboat out of the seaside museum at 4 a.m. for one last row to the lighthouse, oars clacking out of time until they find the old rhythm, and the final splash page shows them rowing straight into the sunrise while the museum alarm rings unheard on shore.
quotes.notes: Excerpt: the closing 15 lines.

quotes.text:
As we come marching, marching, in the beauty of the day,
A million darkened kitchens, a thousand mill-lofts gray
Are touched with all the radiance that a sudden sun discloses,
For the people hear us singing, "Bread and Roses, Bread and Roses."

As we come marching, we battle, too, for men—
For they are women's children and we mother them again.
Our lives shall not be sweated from birth until life closes—
Hearts starve as well as bodies; Give us Bread, but give us Roses!
quotes.author: James Oppenheim
quotes.work: Bread and Roses (first published in The American Magazine, Dec 1911; text as in Poems for Workers, 1925)
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1911; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: A night-shift sewing-machinist in a grey garment factory smuggles a single paper rose onto her machine every night; the supervisor bins it, she makes another, then two appear on the next machine, and the final spread shows the whole floor blooming as the women walk out into the morning.
quotes.notes: The 1925 anthology prints two stanzas; the 1911 original has four. Linked to the 1912 Lawrence textile strike.

quotes.text:
I've known rivers:
I've known rivers ancient as the world and older than the flow of human blood in human veins.

My soul has grown deep like the rivers.

I bathed in the Euphrates when dawns were young.
I built my hut near the Congo and it lulled me to sleep.
I looked upon the Nile and raised the pyramids above it.
I heard the singing of the Mississippi when Abe Lincoln went down to New Orleans, and I've seen its muddy bosom turn all golden in the sunset.

I've known rivers:
Ancient, dusky rivers.

My soul has grown deep like the rivers.
quotes.author: Langston Hughes
quotes.work: The Negro Speaks of Rivers (The Crisis, June 1921; collected in The Weary Blues, 1926)
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1921 and 1926, both before 1929, so public domain in the US (the author died in 1967, so it may still be in copyright in life+70 countries).
quotes.story_seed: A 17-year-old Black busboy crossing the Mississippi on a St. Louis streetcar bridge at sunset looks down, and the river carries him panel by panel through the Euphrates, the Congo and the Nile before he lands back on the tram with a napkin, writing.
quotes.notes: Hughes wrote it at 17 while crossing the Mississippi by train. Public domain in the US by publication date only.

quotes.text: "Let me tell you what I think of bicycling," Miss Anthony said, leaning forward and laying a slender hand on my arm. "I think it has done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world. I stand and rejoice every time I see a woman ride by on a wheel. It gives woman a feeling of freedom and self-reliance. It makes her feel as if she were independent. The moment she takes her seat she knows she can't get into harm unless she gets off her bicycle, and away she goes, the picture of free, untrammeled womanhood."
quotes.popular_text: Let me tell you what I think of bicycling. I think it has done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world. ... the picture of free, untrammeled womanhood.
quotes.author: Susan B. Anthony (interviewed by Nellie Bly)
quotes.work: 'Champion of Her Sex', New York World, 2 Feb 1896
quotes.verification_level: primary transcription on a reliable site
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1896; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: In a 1896 small town a teenage girl in heavy skirts watches the lady doctor whizz past on a bicycle; she trades her mother's churn butter for a rusted frame, falls repeatedly behind the chapel, and the turn is her first downhill run, where the skirts, corset laces and town gossip literally peel away behind her into the wind.
quotes.notes: Interview wording as transcribed from the World article. Wikiquote reads 'It gives women', but the transcription reads 'It gives woman'.

quotes.text: You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.
quotes.author: Frederick Douglass
quotes.work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave, ch. X
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1845; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: A 16-year-old farmhand in 1833 Maryland collapses fanning wheat under a notorious 'slave-breaker'; the story builds to the two-hour fight in the barn where he refuses to be beaten again, the barn walls pulling wider in every panel, and ends with him walking out standing a full head taller in the frame.
quotes.notes: Chapter-turning line of the Narrative. The popular 'I prayed for twenty years... prayed with my legs' is not traceable to Douglass and was dropped.

quotes.text: But the effect of her being on those around her was incalculably diffusive: for the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts; and that things are not so ill with you and me as they might have been, is half owing to the number who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs.
quotes.author: George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans)
quotes.work: Middlemarch, Finale
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1872; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: The comic follows one battered library book through ninety years of date stamps, each stamp a panel of a different borrower's hands, until it reaches the girl who becomes the surgeon on the front page; the final panel pulls back to an overgrown grave of the unnamed librarian who once pulled it from the skip.
quotes.notes: The popular 'It is never too late to be what you might have been' is not found in Eliot's works and was dropped.

quotes.text: From the age of six, I had a mania for drawing the forms of things. By the time I was fifty, I had published an infinity of designs, but all I have produced before the age of seventy is not worth taking into account. At seventy-five I have learned a little about the real structure of nature,—of animals, plants and trees, birds, fishes and insects. In consequence, when I am eighty, I shall have made still more progress. At ninety I shall penetrate the mystery of things; at a hundred I shall certainly have reached a marvellous stage, and when I am a hundred and ten, everything I do—be it but a line or dot—will be alive.
quotes.popular_text: At a hundred and ten, every dot and every line will be alive.
quotes.author: Katsushika Hokusai
quotes.work: Afterword to One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji (Fugaku Hyakkei), tr. in Dora Amsden, Impressions of Ukiyo-ye (1905)
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Japanese original 1834; English translation published 1905 (Amsden). Both public domain.
quotes.story_seed: A 74-year-old retired signwriter joins a beginners' life-drawing class full of art students and draws the same lopsided horse every Tuesday; the pages jump forward in decades until, at his 110th birthday party in the care home, one brushstroke of his horse gallops off the paper and out the window.

zp_adapted_quote.note: Not adapted by Zen Pencils, but already made into this project's own comic 'Every Line Alive'.

quotes.notes: Already adapted by this project as 'Every Line Alive' (scratch/2026-09-27-zen-pencils/README.md). Not adapted by Zen Pencils (Hokusai only appears in a reader comment on the Asimov comic). Several translations exist; Amsden's is the public-domain one.

quotes.text:
A noiseless patient spider,
I mark'd where on a little promontory it stood isolated,
Mark'd how to explore the vacant vast surrounding,
It launch'd forth filament, filament, filament, out of itself,
Ever unreeling them, ever tirelessly speeding them.

And you O my soul where you stand,
Surrounded, detached, in measureless oceans of space,
Ceaselessly musing, venturing, throwing, seeking the spheres to connect them,
Till the bridge you will need be form'd, till the ductile anchor hold,
Till the gossamer thread you fling catch somewhere, O my soul.
quotes.author: Walt Whitman
quotes.work: A Noiseless Patient Spider (Leaves of Grass, 1881-82 text)
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1868 (this text 1881-82); all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: A widowed Korean grandmother newly moved into a silent London block throws out small threads (a wave, kimchi left on a doorstep, a note in bad English) that each fail, drawn as strands of silk drifting in the stairwell, until one lands on the boy in 4B, who knocks with an empty, washed jar.
quotes.notes: Zen Pencils adapted two other Whitman poems (#45, #88), not this one.

quotes.text: I do not know what I may appear to the world, but to myself I seem to have been only like a boy playing on the sea-shore, and diverting myself in now and then finding a smoother pebble or a prettier shell than ordinary, whilst the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered before me.
quotes.author: Isaac Newton (reported)
quotes.work: Reported shortly before his death; printed in Joseph Spence's Anecdotes (1820) and David Brewster, Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton (1855), vol. II ch. 27
quotes.verification_level: secondary: a sourced Wikiquote entry citing the primary source
quotes.public_domain_reason: Printed in 1820 and 1855; public domain.
quotes.story_seed: A world-famous physicist, 90 and frail, slips away from her own gala dinner to a cold beach below the hotel and spends the night in evening dress turning over pebbles by torchlight with a small boy who doesn't know who she is; the last panel is an ocean so large it runs off every edge of the page.

zp_adapted_quote.note: #152 is a science poster titled with Newton's 'shoulders of giants' line; it does not use the seashore quote.

quotes.notes: Recorded second-hand (the source is Newton's nephew-in-law John Conduitt), not written by Newton. Zen Pencils #152 (science poster) uses Newton's different 'shoulders of giants' line as its title; this quote is not adapted.

quotes.text: in every human Breast, God has implanted a Principle, which we call Love of Freedom; it is impatient of Oppression, and pants for Deliverance
quotes.author: Phillis Wheatley
quotes.work: Letter to the Rev. Samson Occom, 11 Feb 1774 (printed in the Connecticut Gazette, March 1774)
quotes.verification_level: primary transcription on a reliable site
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1774; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: A 20-year-old enslaved poet in 1774 Boston writes by candlelight a letter that will be printed in the newspapers; the comic cuts between her quill and a caged goldfinch in the parlour that keeps battering the bars, and ends the morning the paper is sold on the street, with the cage door found open.
quotes.notes: Mid-sentence excerpt (the sentence starts 'I do not say they would have been contented without it, by no means, for...').

quotes.text: I have as much muscle as any man, and can do as much work as any man. I have plowed and reaped and husked and chopped and mowed, and can any man do more than that?
quotes.author: Sojourner Truth
quotes.work: Speech at the Woman's Rights Convention, Akron, Ohio, 1851, as reported by Marius Robinson in the Anti-Slavery Bugle, 21 June 1851
quotes.verification_level: primary transcription on a reliable site
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1851; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: At a village fair's strongman booth that only lets men try, an old farm woman in a bonnet silently rolls up her sleeves and, one by one, out-ploughs, out-reaps and out-chops the hired champion in a harvest contest drawn like a boxing bout, then collects the prize purse and hands it to the girls watching from the fence.
quotes.notes: The famous 'Ain't I a Woman?' refrain comes from Frances Gage's 1863 version, published twelve years later and written in a Southern dialect Truth (a New Yorker whose first language was Dutch) did not speak. The 1851 Robinson report is considered closer to what she said.

quotes.text: If there is no struggle there is no progress. Those who profess to favor freedom and yet deprecate agitation are men who want crops without plowing up the ground; they want rain without thunder and lightning. They want the ocean without the awful roar of its many waters.
quotes.author: Frederick Douglass
quotes.work: West India Emancipation speech, Canandaigua, New York, 3 Aug 1857
quotes.verification_level: primary transcription on a reliable site
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1857; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: At a polite town-hall meeting where every speaker wants 'change, but quietly', drawn as rows of tiny potted plants, a young cleaner takes the microphone, and with each of her sentences the chamber turns into a ploughed field, then a thunderstorm, then a roaring sea that washes the potted plants out the door.
quotes.notes: Continues: 'Power concedes nothing without a demand.'

quotes.text: L'important dans la vie ce n'est point le triomphe mais le combat. L'essentiel ce n'est pas d'avoir vaincu mais de s'être bien battu.
quotes.popular_text: The most important thing in the Olympic Games is not winning but taking part.
quotes.author: Pierre de Coubertin
quotes.work: Speech at a British Government banquet, London Olympic Games, 24 July 1908
quotes.english_gloss: The important thing in life is not the triumph but the struggle. The essential thing is not to have won but to have fought well.
quotes.verification_level: primary transcription on a reliable site
quotes.public_domain_reason: Spoken and printed in 1908; author died 1937. Public domain.
quotes.story_seed: The last-placed runner in a school sports day, a boy with a leg brace, is still on the track as groundskeepers start stacking chairs; the winner, heading home, turns back and runs the final 100 metres beside him, and the last panel is the empty finish line tape strung up again just for them.
quotes.notes: Coubertin was building on a sermon by Bishop Ethelbert Talbot (19 July 1908). The popular 'taking part' line is the Olympic Creed's later form.

quotes.text: I always have a comfortable feeling that nothing is impossible if one applies a certain amount of energy in the right direction. When I want things done, which is always at the last moment, and I am met with such an answer: "It's too late. I hardly think it can be done;" I simply say: "Nonsense! If you want to do it, you can do it. The question is, do you want to do it?"
quotes.author: Nellie Bly (Elizabeth Cochrane Seaman)
quotes.work: Around the World in Seventy-Two Days
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1890; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: A 25-year-old reporter is told at 5 p.m. that the steamer leaves at 9 a.m. and no dressmaker can make her a travelling dress in time; the comic is a frantic one-night montage of her talking a tailor, a trunk-maker and a ticket clerk into 'yes', ending with her waving from the deck in a dress still pinned at the hem.

quotes.text: Had we lived, I should have had a tale to tell of the hardihood, endurance, and courage of my companions which would have stirred the heart of every Englishman. These rough notes and our dead bodies must tell the tale
quotes.author: Robert Falcon Scott
quotes.work: 'Message to the Public', Scott's Last Expedition vol. I (written March 1912)
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1913; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: A teenage care-home volunteer, told to read to a silent old man, finds a frost-stained notebook in his drawer and reads aloud the story of three friends who never came down from a Himalayan col; only at the end does she realise he was the fourth man, sent back for help, who has spent sixty years as the 'rough notes'.
quotes.notes: Excerpt ends mid-sentence ('...must tell the tale, but surely, surely...').

quotes.text: Results! Why, man, I have gotten a lot of results! I know several thousand things that won't work.
quotes.popular_text: I have not failed. I've just found 10,000 ways that won't work.
quotes.author: Thomas A. Edison (reported by Walter S. Mallory)
quotes.work: Frank Lewis Dyer & Thomas Commerford Martin, Edison: His Life and Inventions, vol. II
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1910; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: A 12-year-old trying to rebuild her late grandmother's sourdough loaf pins every failed loaf's photo to the fridge until the door disappears; her dad calls it a waste, and the turn is a page where she reads the fridge like a map, crossing off each failure, before the last photo shows the perfect crumb.
quotes.notes: The popular '10,000 ways' wording is a later paraphrase; Quote Investigator traces the Mallory anecdote.

quotes.text: We especially need imagination in science. It is not all mathematics, nor all logic, but it is somewhat beauty and poetry.
quotes.author: Maria Mitchell
quotes.work: Maria Mitchell: Life, Letters, and Journals, ed. Phebe Mitchell Kendall
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1896; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: A girl failing algebra is sent to rooftop 'detention' with the school janitor, who turns out to have a homemade telescope; her margin doodles of lunar craters slowly turn into measurements, and the last panel shows her at 40 in an observatory dome, the janitor's telescope on a shelf behind her.
quotes.notes: Mitchell discovered a comet in 1847 and was the first American woman professional astronomer.

quotes.text: I yearn to be with those who reach the South Pole, the lure of the Arctic is tugging at my heart, to me the trail is calling! "The Old Trail! The Trail that is always New!"
quotes.author: Matthew A. Henson
quotes.work: A Negro Explorer at the North Pole
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition

quotes.text:
Not like the brazen giant of Greek fame,
With conquering limbs astride from land to land;
Here at our sea-washed, sunset gates shall stand
A mighty woman with a torch, whose flame
Is the imprisoned lightning, and her name
Mother of Exiles. From her beacon-hand
Glows world-wide welcome; her mild eyes command
The air-bridged harbor that twin cities frame.
"Keep, ancient lands, your storied pomp!" cries she
With silent lips. "Give me your tired, your poor,
Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free,
The wretched refuse of your teeming shore.
Send these, the homeless, tempest-tost to me,
I lift my lamp beside the golden door!"
quotes.author: Emma Lazarus

quotes.text:
The heart of a woman goes forth with the dawn,
As a lone bird, soft winging, so restlessly on,
Afar o'er life's turrets and vales does it roam
In the wake of those echoes the heart calls home.

The heart of a woman falls back with the night,
And enters some alien cage in its plight,
And tries to forget it has dreamed of the stars
While it breaks, breaks, breaks on the sheltering bars.
quotes.author: Georgia Douglas Johnson
quotes.work: The Heart of a Woman (The Heart of a Woman and Other Poems, 1918)

quotes.notes: Harlem Renaissance poet. Complete poem, 8 lines. It is sad rather than triumphant, so a comic would need to supply the turn.

quotes.text:
I know why the caged bird sings, ah me,
   When his wing is bruised and his bosom sore,—
When he beats his bars and he would be free;
It is not a carol of joy or glee,
   But a prayer that he sends from his heart's deep core,
But a plea, that upward to Heaven he flings—
I know why the caged bird sings!

Nor all thy Tears wash out a Word of it.

quotes.text:
We cannot keep the gold of yesterday;
To-day's dun clouds we cannot roll away.
Now the long, wailing flight of geese brings autumn in its train,
So to the view-tower cup in hand to fill and drink again,
And dream of the greatest singers of the past,
Their fadeless lines of fire and beauty cast.
I too have felt the wild-bird thrill of song behind the bars,
But these have brushed the world aside and walked amid the stars.
In vain we cleave the torrent's thread with steel,
In vain we drink to drown the grief we feel;
When man's desire with fate doth war this, this avails alone—
To hoist the sail and let the gale and the waters bear us on.

quotes.text:
Hope is the thing with feathers
That perches in the soul,
And sings the tune without the words,
And never stops at all,

And sweetest in the gale is heard;
And sore must be the storm
That could abash the little bird
That kept so many warm.

I've heard it in the chillest land,
And on the strangest sea;
Yet, never, in extremity,
It asked a crumb of me.
quotes.popular_text:
"Hope" is the thing with feathers -
That perches in the soul -
And sings the tune without the words -
And never stops - at all - ...

quotes.text:
It's easy to cry that you're beaten — and die;
It's easy to crawfish and crawl;
But to fight and to fight when hope's out of sight —
Why, that's the best game of them all!
And though you come out of each gruelling bout,
All broken and beaten and scarred,
Just have one more try — it's dead easy to die,
It's the keeping-on-living that's hard.

quotes.text:
If we must die, let it not be like hogs
Hunted and penned in an inglorious spot,
While round us bark the mad and hungry dogs,
Making their mock at our accursèd lot.
If we must die, O let us nobly die,
So that our precious blood may not be shed
In vain; then even the monsters we defy
Shall be constrained to honor us though dead!
O kinsmen! we must meet the common foe!
Though far outnumbered let us show us brave,
And for their thousand blows deal one death-blow!
What though before us lies the open grave?
Like men we'll face the murderous, cowardly pack,
Pressed to the wall, dying, but fighting back!
quotes.author: Claude McKay
quotes.work: If We Must Die (The Liberator, July 1919; Harlem Shadows, 1922)

quotes.story_seed: During the Red Summer of 1919, a Jamaican-born railway dining-car waiter hears of riots at every stop; he hides a family in the pantry car, and the whole waiting staff link arms across the door as a mob boards, drawn in woodcut blacks.
quotes.notes: Written in response to the Red Summer of 1919. It is defiant and violent rather than gentle, so it suits a darker comic.

quotes.text:
No coward soul is mine,
No trembler in the world's storm-troubled sphere:
I see Heaven's glories shine,
And faith shines equal, arming me from fear.
quotes.author: Emily Brontë
quotes.work: No Coward Soul Is Mine (written 1846; published 1850), stanza 1
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition

quotes.story_seed: A timid parish clerk's daughter on the Yorkshire moors shepherds a lost flock alone through a night storm, the sky tearing open in panel after panel, and walks into the village at dawn soaked but upright while the men who were too scared to go are still arguing in the pub doorway.

quotes.text: I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.
quotes.author: Mary Wollstonecraft
quotes.work: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, ch. IV
quotes.verification_level: primary: digitised text of the original or early edition
quotes.public_domain_reason: Published 1792; all works published before 1929 are public domain in the US.
quotes.story_seed: A girl who is only allowed to sweep in her father's 1790s London print shop sets type for her own pamphlet one letter a night; the turn is that she never publishes it but reads it aloud to herself in the dark shop, and next morning walks up to her father and asks for wages.
quotes.notes: Responding to Rousseau, who is quoted just before this line.
